entries.title: OCP Summit 2026: Powering AI with Open Innovations in Scale-Up, Scale-Out, and Scale-Across Networks
entries.summary: At the 2026 Open Compute Project Global Summit, Meta is sharing the next generation of open networking infrastructure, including: Our first liquid-cooled network rack (IcePack), and 102.4T switch platform (IceCube). Flattened Planar Fabric (FPF), a multiplane backend scale-out fabric that fundamentally changes how GPUs connect to the network MetaRoCE, our open-source AI transport protocol. Launchi
entries.content:
• At the 2026 Open Compute Project Global Summit, Meta is sharing the next generation of open networking infrastructure, including: 
    • Our first liquid-cooled network rack (IcePack), and 102.4T switch platform (IceCube).
    • Flattened Planar Fabric (FPF), a multiplane backend scale-out fabric that fundamentally changes how GPUs connect to the network
    • MetaRoCE, our open-source AI transport protocol.
    • Launching the Open Switch Platform Architecture (OSPA) initiative within OCP.
  • We’re inviting engineers, silicon vendors, system integrators, and operators to join us and the OCP community in meeting the challenges of building open, efficient, and sustainable AI infrastructure.

At Meta, we believe that open networking is critical for building high-performance, scalable, and sustainable infrastructure, and we’ve acted on that conviction since co-founding the Open Compute Project (OCP) in 2011.

Throughout the ongoing AI revolution, Meta has pushed the boundaries of what’s possible in data center networking and shared our advances with the industry. At OCP 2025, we introduced our latest AI scale-out fabrics and drove the creation of the Ethernet for Scale-Up Networking (ESUN) initiative.

This year at OCP 2026, we’re sharing the networking innovations that directly support our latest AI workloads such as Meta’s Muse Wonder and Muse Spark models, and Muse, our personal AI agent built for everyone. Here’s some of what’s new:

  • The 102.4T scale-out switch: Meta’s first liquid-cooled network rack (IcePack) and 102.4T switch blades (IceCube), designed to support high power density, deliver higher thermal efficiency, and enable gigawatt-scale AI clusters.
  • The scale-out Flattened Planar Fabric (FPF): Meta’s multiplane fabric, enabling larger, highly efficient GPU clusters with lower latency — with learnings shared with our cloud partners.
  • Scale-across for multi-site clusters: Meta’s petabit-scale backend aggregation (BAG) super-spine and how large-scale training jobs deal with failures at this scale — with an overview of how we’ve built SRv6 regional backbones using FBOSS and SAI to handle even longer distances
  • Ethernet for Scale-Up Networking: Meta’s MTIA 300 system uses Tahan, an Ethernet-based 51.2T scale-up switch, delivering 6.4 Tbps per accelerator — with a preview of next-gen 72-accelerator-per-rack design on 102.4T silicon and moving toward an ESUN-based implementation with future chips.
  • Open Switch Platform Architecture (OSPA): a new OCP initiative, co-led by Meta, Microsoft, and Alibaba, that standardizes the switch platform layer — with specification v1.0 now submitted to OCP.
  • MetaRoCE: Meta’s RDMA transport protocol for AI networks — now with open-source implementations.

The 102.4T Generation: Liquid-Cooled Networking at AI Scale

As AI clusters grow to gigawatt scale, network switches must deliver dramatically more bandwidth while fitting within increasingly dense power and cooling envelopes. Our answer is the IcePack rack, Meta’s first-generation liquid-cooled network rack.

IcePack is based on OCP’s ORV3-HPRv1 rack standard. IceCube switch blades — 102.4-Tbps fabric switches that deliver 128×800G non-blocking switching capacity — sit inside each rack. IceCube comes in two variants, one built on Broadcom’s Tomahawk6C switch ASIC and one on NVIDIA Spectrum-6 Switch ASIC. Both run Meta’s open-source FBOSS network operating system that leverages OCP SAI (Switch Abstraction Interface). 

This new generation represents a 2x bandwidth increase over our 51.2T platforms while achieving the thermal density required for next-generation AI data centers.

Scaling AI Fabrics From Building to Region

As seen at Meta and across the industry, AI clusters now span buildings, campuses, and multiple regions. This demands fabric architectures that are not only massive in scale but also resilient and flexible.

Flattened Planar Fabric (FPF): More Resilient, Larger Clusters

We’re introducing Flattened Planar Fabric (FPF), Meta’s multiplane backend scale-out fabric that fundamentally changes how GPUs connect to the network and the network control plane of the fabric.

With FPF, each GPU connects via eight independent 100G links to eight different switches (one per network plane). This multiplane approach replaces the traditional single-plane uplink architecture and delivers four key advantages:

  • Larger non-blocking GPU clusters compared to single-plane topologies, which enables the scale required for our largest AI training workloads
  • A flattened topology, moving from the 3-tier Clos fabric of our NSF fabric to a 2-tier Clos fabric. Removing this tier of switches reduces network hops, latency, and infrastructure cost.
  • NIC-level hardware load balancing: Load balancing, traditionally done by network switches, now starts at the NIC, which sprays every packet across all eight planes in hardware.
  • A combined control plane for fault tolerance: The control plane of FPF includes both the switches and the hosts, allowing the host to steer traffic away from downed planes.

Meta collaborated closely with NVIDIA on developing FPF running inside Meta’s infrastructure, leveraging NVIDIA Spectrum-X Multiplane innovations to ensure FPF has high performance even under assorted failure conditions and operational lifecycle scenarios. Going beyond our own infrastructure, Meta and NVIDIA have been working closely with our joint cloud partners to help standardize multiplane fabrics implementations within those partners based on our FPF learnings.

Bridging On-Prem Data Centers and Public Cloud

This work with cloud providers on FPF is just one example of how we at Meta are not just building our own infrastructure, but are helping our partners’ infrastructure.

Our ambitions for scaling our AI capacity cannot be met by building data centers alone, because construction runs on multi-year lead times while demand moves in months. So we use leased facilities and public cloud capacity, alongside our own campuses, to close the gap. But it only works if the network behaves the same way no matter where the GPUs sit.

That is genuinely difficult, because cloud networking is not the same as owning the rack. Fabric topologies differ from provider to provider rather than following one uniform design. Buffering is often shallower, which changes congestion and loss behavior. RDMA transports are provider-specific, and some clouds still run InfiniBand rather than Ethernet and RoCE. What works for a handful of cloud instances also tends to break at fleet scale.

At OCP we’re sharing how we’re converging these environments into a single operational model. That includes a standardized performance validation framework — cloud partners run a common suite of point-to-point and collective benchmarks, scaling from tens to over a thousand GPUs, before a cluster is ever handed over, so performance is proven rather than assumed. It includes normalizing heterogeneous, often multiplane fabrics, mapping divergent traffic-class schemes and congestion-control parameters onto our lossless RDMA classes so end-to-end paths behave predictably across different vendors’ NICs and switches.

The principle we keep applying is that heterogeneity is manageable but standardization is what makes it affordable. Testing and qualification, RDMA transport and congestion behavior, and telemetry all still diverge across providers, and every divergence becomes engineering work.

BAG: Scale-Across Aggregation

The scale of AI capacity Meta has committed to this decade — Prometheus at roughly 1 gigawatt in 2026, and Hyperion scaling toward 5 gigawatts— means a single cluster now outgrows any single region. Our backend aggregation (BAG) layer is a centralized, Ethernet-based super-spine that interconnects many spine-layer fabrics into one mega cluster spanning buildings, campuses, and regions. It operates at petabit scale — inter-BAG capacity between a pair of regions reaches tens of petabits per second. BAG is what allows Prometheus to function as a single cluster even though its capacity is spread across conventional data center buildings, weatherproof outdoor structures, and adjacent colocation space.

At this reach, distance itself becomes a design constraint. Lossless Ethernet requires buffer headroom proportional to cable length, so once links stretch tens of kilometers, buffer management turns into a first-order problem rather than a tuning detail. And getting it wrong risks congestion spreading well beyond the link that caused it. Instead of provisioning every link for a worst-case distance, FBOSS now measures actual cable length in place, timing probe traffic on an uncongested queue to derive round-trip distance, and allocates headroom against the measurement.

Load balancing also has to reason about paths that are degraded rather than simply down. BAG uses eBGP link-bandwidth signaling so traffic is distributed in proportion to the capacity actually available on each path, with deliberate damping so that a single link failure does not ripple routing churn across the domain. And because inter-fabric latency is several times intra-fabric latency, collective communication libraries — which generally choose algorithms without any awareness of network distance — can fall off a performance cliff.

We’ve been addressing that from both directions, with adaptive routing improvements to reduce the latency penalty and scheduling that minimizes how much collective traffic needs to cross the BAG layer at all. Training remains resilient throughout. When a replica fails, it is automatically excluded and the surviving replicas continue synchronizing across BAG.

The direction of travel is longer distances still — training jobs spanning regions tens, hundreds, or thousands of kilometers apart — and increasingly heterogeneous clusters that mix hardware generations and vendors.

SRv6-Powered Regional Backbone Using FBOSS

We’ve deployed Segment Routing over IPv6 (SRv6) using FBOSS for our regional backbone networks. This enables more flexible traffic engineering and simplified operations as we interconnect AI clusters across geographies — running on open shallow-buffer switch platforms powered by Cisco SiliconOne, with ongoing work to onboard additional silicon families, all managed under FBOSS using OCP SAI.

Ethernet for Scale-Up: Our Commitment to Ethernet

A defining milestone of OCP 2026 is proving that Ethernet can serve the scale-up domain — the high-bandwidth, ultra-low-latency interconnects between accelerators within a rack or pod that have traditionally required proprietary technologies.

Tahan: Ethernet-Based Scale-Up Switch

We’re introducing Tahan, Meta’s Ethernet-based scale-up switch — purpose-built for our MTIA 300 training accelerators. Tahan is built on the 51.2 Tbps Tomahawk 5 ASIC from Broadcom, offering total capacity of 64x800G, half of which is used to provide scale-up connectivity to the accelerators via the backplane. Four Tahan switches interconnect 16 accelerators in a non-blocking topology.

Importantly, Tahan reuses the same lossless RoCE transport (routed IPv6, PFC, AI-tuned QoS) as our scale-out network, unifying both scale-up and scale-out fabrics under FBOSS.

Next-Generation Scale-Up: 72 Accelerators per Rack on 102.4T Silicon

We’re also previewing the next-generation scale-up blade, a 216×400G switch built on 102.4 Tbps Broadcom Tomahawk6C silicon. Eight of these switches interconnect 72 accelerators per rack, a dramatic increase in density enabled by the bandwidth of the 102.4T generation. A future generation of this scale-up blade is planned to adopt OCP Ethernet for Scale-Up Networking (ESUN) as the scale-up data plane, cementing our commitment to open standards for the entire scale-up stack.

ESUN Evolving

The ESUN initiative we founded within OCP last year has made significant progress. Working alongside AMD, Arista, ARM, Broadcom, Cisco, HPE, Marvell, Microsoft, and NVIDIA, ESUN is advancing open specifications for:

  • Protocol headers and framing optimized for scale-up topologies.
  • Error handling mechanisms for lossless multi-hop fabrics.
  • Alignment with UEC and IEEE standards.

This work has already produced a concrete result with the ESUN 1.0 Network Operator Requirements Base Specification released earlier this year. ESUN 1.0 deliberately focuses on the fabric, defining what the network must deliver while leaving implementation flexibility to GPU and accelerator vendors, which broadens adoption. It also coordinates with existing standards bodies, leveraging work underway in IEEE and the Ultra Ethernet Consortium (UEC) rather than duplicating it.

Since publishing ESUN 1.0, the group is now close to the next version, ESUN 1.1, tackling new features such as switch profiles and inter-packet gap reduction that further optimize Ethernet for low-latency, scale-up use cases.

With Tahan shipping today, a 72-accelerator-per-rack design on the horizon adopting ESUN as its data plane, and ESUN continuing to evolve its open specifications, we’re helping build a complete open platform for the scale-up future.

Ecosystem Enablement and Open Transport

Our commitment to openness extends across the full networking stack — from switch platform hardware to transport protocols.

OSPA: Open Switch Platform Architecture

SAI made switch data plane software portable across silicon. But the layer beneath it, the switch platform layer, has remained proprietary and fragmented. Every new hardware platform requires months of duplicated, custom engineering to bring up, and a lack of standard platform design multiplies long-term maintenance and troubleshooting cost. In an era of compressed AI hardware cycles, that onboarding tax has become untenable.

To fix this, we’re co-leading a new OCP initiative with Microsoft and Alibaba, the Open Switch Platform Architecture (OSPA) — a unified reference design for the switch platform layer. 

OSPA standardizes the hardware and software interfaces for:

  • Power management and power sequencing.
  • Sensor and environment control, including thermal and fan management.
  • Hardware inventory management and device enumeration.
  • Out-of-band hardware interfaces (management Ethernet, serial console, USB, LED indicators).
  • Firmware maintenance and updates.
  • Platform troubleshooting and diagnostics.

FBOSS Ecosystem Enablement

Over the past year we made a major push to extend open-source FBOSS so that switch vendors can self-onboard their own platforms without Meta engineers in the loop for the port. The goal is a self-service model in which multiple new switch platforms can be developed concurrently, giving vendors access to a hyperscale-proven NOS as they build FBOSS-compatible hardware.

Vendors and developers can get started at the FBOSS documentation site and the FBOSS GitHub repository.

MetaRoCE: Open-Source Transport for AI Clusters

As we recently announced, MetaRoCE is our open-source RDMA transport protocol optimized for AI cluster networks over Ethernet. MetaRoCE provides the congestion control and reliability semantics that distributed AI training workloads demand. It’s purpose-built for the unique traffic patterns of collective communication across large-scale Ethernet fabrics. 

At OCP, we are announcing our open-source MetaRoCE implementations, enabling the broader AI infrastructure community to adopt and build upon a production-proven transport stack.

Join Us in Building the Open Future of AI Networking

The pace of AI infrastructure evolution continues to accelerate. The challenges of building open, efficient, and sustainable AI networking are too large for any single company to solve alone.

We invite engineers, silicon vendors, system integrators, and operators to join us and the OCP community in defining what comes next. Visit our presentations at OCP 2026, explore our open-source contributions including FBOSS and MetaRoCE, and collaborate with us on building the networking infrastructure the AI era demands.

The authors are members of the Network Infrastructure team at Meta.

entries.title: Shipping Media Over QUIC at Meta Scale for Instagram Live Ingest
entries.summary: Meta has begun deploying Media over QUIC (MoQ), an emerging open protocol for real-time video streaming at scale. MoQ will help simplify our protocol stack for live streaming video and enhance overall user experience for live video. We’re sharing how we shipped MoQ on Instagram Live ingest, and what the future looks like from here. [...] Read More... The post Shipping Media Over QUIC at Meta Scale
entries.content:
• Meta has begun deploying Media over QUIC (MoQ), an emerging open protocol for real-time video streaming at scale.
  • MoQ will help simplify our protocol stack for live streaming video and enhance overall user experience for live video.
  • We’re sharing how we shipped MoQ on Instagram Live ingest, and what the future looks like from here.
  • This work was also presented at DEMOQED 2026.

Instagram Live now uses the open standard transport protocol Media over QUIC (MoQ) for live video ingest on iOS and Android. As a transport designed for both ingest and playback, MoQ gives us the foundation to build toward an architecture that is lower-latency, more resilient on unreliable networks, and more responsive for creators and viewers. It also gives teams across Meta a common foundation for bringing those improvements to future live and interactive experiences without rebuilding them on separate protocol stacks.

MoQ: A Media Protocol for Every Moment in Time

The internet has accumulated a rich set of media protocols, each shaped by the problem in front of it. RTMP for ingestion. HLS and DASH for playback. WebRTC for real-time calls. RUSH for the cases that did not fit neatly into any of those. Each was a strong answer for its moment, and together they’ve carried the industry a long way. At Meta, someone who starts a live stream and then makes a voice call on the same app touches three different protocol stacks, each with its own serving infrastructure, monitoring, and operational expertise. 

That separation made sense when these experiences were distinct. But as live video, real-time AI, and generative AI creation tools increasingly share the same product surface, the lines between these use cases are starting to blur. A common protocol across ingest, delivery, and playback can reduce the number of custom transports and operating models that engineering teams need to maintain and improve over time.

How MoQ Works

MoQ is an emerging IETF standard that enables low-latency, scalable media delivery (live streaming, real-time communication) over the QUIC transport layer. It’s being developed collaboratively at the IETF, with active participation from Meta, Google, Akamai, Cisco, Cloudflare, and academia.

For nearly a decade, Meta’s live streaming video has run on Reliable Ultra-low-latency Streaming over HTTP (RUSH), an in-house QUIC-based protocol built to move past RTMP. RUSH proved that QUIC could carry live media at scale and was a predecessor to MoQ. The lessons learned from running RUSH in production are part of what shaped our bet on MoQ.

The core abstraction in MoQ is a Track, an addressable stream of media objects that publishers push and subscribers receive through a network of relays. Relays cache and forward objects without parsing the media payload – they only need to understand the MoQ framing and delivery metadata.

A few properties matter for using MoQ as a single transport across the full latency spectrum:

  • Built on QUIC: QUIC lets independent streams make progress without TCP-style cross-stream head-of-line blocking. It also supports faster connection setup and connection migration. Meta’s earlier QUIC rollout achieved lower request errors, tail latency, and video stalls than HTTP/2. MoQ applies the same transport foundation to live and real-time media. MoQ would also automatically benefit from any feature added to QUIC (e.g., FEC). 
  • Native Fan-out and caching: MoQ relays are built-in caching and request/stream coalescing endpoints, so media streams scale through CDN relays out of the box. Request coalescing, caching, and fan-out are not new (live streaming already does them), but MoQ makes them part of the protocol design rather than a bolt-on, and it is designed to scale via relays more efficiently than traditional HTTP streaming.
  • Tunable Latency per use case: Two subscribers to the same track can run at different latencies at the same time — e.g., ~100 ms for an interactive participant and several seconds for an archival or buffered service — based on tunable per-subscription delivery properties.
  • Track-aware delivery: Relays can drop, prioritize, or replay objects based on metadata, giving better congestion behavior under loss than byte-stream protocols.
  • First-class media context: Tracks and their quality variants are modeled in the protocol itself, so adaptive bitrate logic is built directly on native MoQ constructs rather than reconstructed at higher layers.
  • Standards-based TCP fallback: When QUIC is blocked, MoQ can fall back to TCP through a standardized mapping (e.g., WebTransport over HTTP/2, or the emerging QMUX mapping), so a blocked network doesn’t force the ecosystem back into multiple parallel transports.

First Deployment at Scale: Instagram Live

Of all the surfaces MoQ can serve at Meta, we chose to ship live video ingest first for three reasons:

Instagram Live is our largest-scale test: Instagram Live serves users at Meta scale. Proving MoQ at this scale clears the bar for the most demanding ingest workloads, and is complementary to the low-latency properties that matter for real-time use cases.

RUSH was falling behind the open ecosystem: Live ingest had been running on RUSH, Meta’s pragmatic QUIC-based answer to RTMP. RUSH was stable and performant at scale for nearly a decade, but the move to MoQ shifts development from a protocol operated primarily by Meta to a shared standards effort. Multiple implementers can contribute experience, test interoperability, and improve the specification instead of Meta evolving the transport largely on its own.

Metric parity is a prerequisite for everything else: Proving MoQ can operate at Meta scale for its largest live surface without regression gives us a clean baseline from which to explore, including live playback among others.

Rolling out MoQ on Instagram Live

Replacing the live ingest protocol on Instagram Live meant changing the foundation under every broadcast on the service. We had to do it without regressions visible to creators or viewers, and without coupling the wire-format change to a rewrite of every downstream system.

Replacing a transport protocol in a live production system is hard for reasons that have little to do with the protocol itself — broadcaster apps need to learn it, the backend pipeline expects the old framing, the rollout has to be reversible in seconds, and a non-trivial slice of networks can’t carry the new transport at all.

We tackled these as three constrained problems:

Client integration across four apps: A MoQ publisher built on moxygen, Meta’s open-source MoQ library, integrated in our apps. moxygen provides publisher, subscriber, and relay roles, integrates with our QUIC stack (mvfst), and exposes hooks for custom media handlers. A single config parameter chooses MoQ or RUSH for a given broadcast.

Translation at the edge instead of rewriting the backend. MoQ ingest connections terminate on dedicated edge endpoints, where a translation layer converts MoQ frames to the RUSH format the existing backend already understands. Nothing downstream changes while we swap the client transport. The translator is temporary scaffolding; once MoQ is the only ingest path, the backend will consume MoQ natively and the shim goes away.

Server-side routing for fast ramps. Stream URL generation routes experiment-eligible broadcasts to MoQ-capable endpoints based on experiment-group membership, so phased rollout doesn’t depend on app-version adoption and the experiment can be resized in minutes.

Operational Hurdles

  • Evolving Specifications: As an active IETF standard, the MoQ draft continued to evolve while we built. We pinned to specific draft versions, kept compatibility shims around for older clients, and contributed improvements back to the IETF working group.
  • Firewalls: UDP/443 is still blocked or rate-limited on a non-trivial slice of enterprise and carrier networks. We pick the transport (TCP or QUIC) at the start of the live stream based on which handshake wins, and go with that for the session.
  • Debugging: QUIC’s encryption hides framing from middleboxes, and from our own packet captures. We built MoQ-aware tracing into the edge so we could see object-level events without decrypting the wire.

The Outcome

After months of experimentation on Instagram iOS and Android, we launched MoQ for Instagram Live ingest. The MoQ path matched RUSH across the streaming-quality indicators and reliability measures used for the rollout.

Achieving parity was the target for this phase, and it showed that we could replace a production transport without disrupting creators or viewers. It also gives the next phase a production-tested transport, rollout controls, and observability.

This now becomes the foundation to extend MoQ to an end-to-end architecture for live video delivery and playback. In that target architecture, media can be pushed as it is produced, and partial reliability can let the player skip stale video after loss instead of allowing delay to accumulate. Adaptive bitrate work can trade resolution for continuity as bandwidth changes. We believe these capabilities will form the basis of the next-generation live video architecture for richer, more responsive experiences for creators and viewers.

What’s Next: Other Explorations Within Meta

Instagram Live is the first MoQ workload at Meta. Reaching parity at Instagram Live scale gives us a clean baseline to ask where else a single QUIC-based transport could collapse a set of special-case stacks into one. The directions below are areas we’re exploring:

Finishing the Live Ingest Story: The next logical steps build on top of what we’ve done — extending MoQ across the rest of Meta’s apps using MoQ-native constructs like subgroups to carry audio, video, and metadata on independent streams for better resilience under loss, and adding a standards-based TCP fallback (QMUX). Today, we lean on RUSH’s existing TCP fallback as an expediency for QUIC-blocked networks; standardizing on QMUX removes that dependency so a blocked network no longer forces a second protocol, eventually opening the door to retire RUSH.

Real-time Interactive AI: Conversational and real-time AI surfaces move architectures toward continuous human-to-server communication. A single low-latency, bidirectional transport that carries signaling and media together is a natural fit. Meeting the latency, loss-recovery, and media quality requirements that real-time communication demands is an area we are actively exploring.

Shipping MoQ for Instagram Live makes this one of the largest application usages of MoQ we are aware of in the industry, both by the number of ingest streams and total volume. An open IETF-standard transport is now carrying media at Meta’s scale, and the future it unlocks is exciting.

Learn More About Meta’s MoQ Deployment

Interested in learning more? Check out the MoQ Transport IETF draft and our moxygen open-source library.

entries.title: Turning Opportunistic AI Inference Capacity Into Better Ads Recommendations
entries.summary: At Meta, we’ve built a system that enhances ads recommendations by leveraging idle inference capacity in our fleet. Two elasticity levers in the system allow ads recommendation work to expand across opportunistic capacity, without compromising baseline performance. This post describes how we designed and now operate the system at Meta’s scale and how it drives [...] Read More... The post Turning O
entries.content:
• At Meta, we’ve built a system that enhances ads recommendations by leveraging idle inference capacity in our fleet.
  • Two elasticity levers in the system allow ads recommendation work to expand across opportunistic capacity, without compromising baseline performance.
  • This post describes how we designed and now operate the system at Meta’s scale and how it drives significant advertiser value and capacity efficiency.

Inference fleets face a capacity paradox: They can be globally constrained while meaningful pockets of capacity remain locally idle. At Meta, we built a system that aggregates these pockets into a shared opportunistic capacity pool and turns them into better ads recommendations. By putting otherwise idle capacity to work, the system helps people see more relevant ads and improves advertiser outcomes without requiring additional capacity orders.

Using this opportunistic capacity safely is difficult. It’s distributed across team-owned capacity allocations, regions, and accelerator types, and may be reclaimed with little notice. The ads inference system must therefore adapt workload as capacity supply changes without overloading the dedicated capacity that serves baseline workload.

We address this challenge with two complementary elasticity levers. Rank More Ads (RMA) adjusts the number of candidates evaluated by the ranking stages. Serve Better Models (SBM) adjusts the share of requests routed to a more powerful model.

Physical and logical isolation protects the capacity reserved for baseline serving. Separate feedback loops control RMA candidate volume and SBM model coverage, while value-aware load shedding at both servers and clients allows the system to degrade gracefully when capacity is suddenly reclaimed. Together, these mechanisms allow optional work to expand and contract with opportunistic capacity while protecting latency and reliability.

The Inference Capacity Paradox: Globally Constrained, but Locally Idle

Inference fleets must maintain enough capacity to meet demand under strict latency and reliability targets. However, demand and capacity rarely align perfectly across time, regions, resource combinations, and accelerator types. Capacity can therefore remain idle in parts of a fleet even when the fleet is constrained overall. Common causes include:

  • Peak-provisioning and demand-variation mismatch: Inference fleets must be provisioned for peak demand, while traffic varies by time of day and season. Capacity needed during peak periods can therefore remain temporarily idle when demand is lower.
  • Model-development and capacity-delivery timing mismatch: Inference capacity arrives on supply-chain timelines, whereas models are developed and launched on separate schedules. This creates a gap between when capacity becomes available and when models are ready to consume it.
  • Regional resource-ratio mismatch: Inference workloads require accelerators as well as supporting resources such as CPUs. When these resources are not available in the required proportions, one resource can remain idle while another limits serving capacity.
  • Accelerator-type mismatch: Inference fleets can span multiple accelerator vendors, generations, and architectures. Workloads are not always portable across these accelerator types, which can strand capacity on hardware that cannot immediately serve the available demand.

These mismatches create an industry-wide inference capacity paradox: A fleet can be globally constrained while meaningful pockets of capacity remain locally idle. At Meta’s scale, these temporary pockets can collectively represent substantial capacity and create better ads recommendations when used safely.

From Fragmented Reservations to a Shared Opportunistic Capacity Pool

Across a heterogeneous fleet at Meta’s scale, instantaneous idle inference capacity is inevitable — even with proactive planning designed to minimize structural mismatches. However, because this capacity is inherently tied to fluctuating baseline demands, it comes with distinct operational constraints — it’s preemptible (can be reclaimed at any time), highly volatile in its availability, and carries no long-term guarantees.

To successfully consume this volatile resource without compromising baseline performance, workloads must exhibit certain structural properties:

  • A high degree of workload elasticity: The workload can quickly add or remove a large amount of optional work as the pool changes without affecting baseline expectations.
  • Sustained quality at scale: The workload can continue to meaningfully improve output quality across the range the opportunistic pool can supply. This type of workload often already uses a large amount of dedicated capacity due to this property.
  • Limited cross-service dependencies: A self-contained workload reduces the number of upstream and downstream systems that must respond to volatile capacity.

Two Complementary Elasticity Levers

Based on these structural properties, we identified two complementary levers that meet these criteria to consume this idle capacity and generate large value upside.

Rank More Ads (RMA)

For each user request, the ads recommendation system must select a small number of ads from millions of candidates in less than a second. The system uses a sequence of ranking stages in which increasingly powerful machine learning models evaluate progressively smaller candidate sets. The later stages only evaluate the top candidates from the previous stage.

RMA increases the number of candidates evaluated by the ranking stages when opportunistic capacity is available. Evaluating more candidates increases the chance of finding ads that are relevant to the user. Because the additional candidates pass through CPU-heavy upstream (e.g., retrieval, feature processing) as well as accelerator-heavy inference, RMA generally requires both CPU and accelerator surplus.

Serve Better Models (SBM)

The ads evaluation can use models with different levels of complexity. More powerful models can improve prediction quality, but it’s not efficient to use them for every request with dedicated capacity.

SBM changes the share of requests evaluated by the more powerful models as accelerator capacity changes. It keeps the number of ads entering the ranking stages constant, so upstream CPU demand remains comparatively stable. This allows SBM to use accelerator-only surplus that RMA cannot consume.

The SBM model-router component uses request-value signals to prioritize the requests expected to benefit most from a more powerful model.

Why Both Levers Are Needed

The two levers consume different combinations of resources. RMA requires both CPU and accelerator capacity, while SBM can use accelerator capacity without substantially increasing upstream CPU work. Together, they can use a broader range of opportunistic capacity than either lever alone.

The incremental impact of each lever also changes with traffic, current coverage, and the available resource mix. At a given moment, the next unit of opportunistic capacity may surface more relevant ads by ranking additional candidates to serve better ads or by routing more requests to a powerful model for improved prediction accuracy. We periodically adjust the allocation between RMA and SBM based on their measured performance and resource requirements.

Safely Using Opportunistic Capacity for Ads Inference

Opportunistic capacity can be reclaimed faster than the control loops that regulate work across a large serving fleet. We therefore design the system around one requirement – losing opportunistic capacity may reduce incremental ranking work, but it must not overload the capacity that serves the baseline workload. We support this requirement through isolated routing targets, two workload-specific feedback loops, and fast local load shedding.

Protecting Baseline Traffic Through Physical and Logical Isolation

Optional work must not consume the capacity reserved for baseline serving. SBM and RMA enforce this separation differently.

For SBM, the isolation is physical. The baseline and more powerful models use separate routing targets. Dedicated replicas are sized to serve requests with the baseline model, while replicas on opportunistic capacity serve requests selected for the more powerful model. When opportunistic capacity contracts, the system reduces the share of requests routed to the more powerful model. Those requests use the baseline model instead, whose capacity is already provisioned for them.

For RMA, the isolation is logical. The system calculates how much additional candidate-ranking work can be supported by the model replicas deployed on opportunistic capacity and uses total capacity to set a global budget for RMA. Each model replica may receive a mixture of baseline and additional work; individual requests do not need to be physically separated. Baseline traffic is protected by limiting the total incremental work to the amount that these replicas can support.

When opportunistic capacity contracts, RMA reduces its global candidate-volume target and SBM reduces its more-powerful-model coverage. In both cases, the system removes optional work rather than allowing it to spill onto the capacity reserved for baseline serving. This keeps baseline traffic within its latency and reliability targets.

Controlling Candidate Volume With Latency Feedback

RMA uses a closed feedback loop composed of a central proportional-integral-derivative (PID) controller and client-side enforcement. Looking through a simplified lens, the controller uses observed tail latency to calculate a target for the number of ads sent to downstream ranking, and clients apply that target to new requests. When latency is below the target, the controller increases the number of ads ranked. When latency rises, it reduces the number. This allows RMA to use the latency signal, which is influenced by the capacity situation, to converge on a sustainable candidate volume as conditions change.

Routing Requests With Value-Aware Model Selection

SBM uses a corresponding feedback loop with central control and client-side routing. The central controller sets the target coverage for the more powerful model, and the client-side model router decides which eligible requests use that model and which continue through the baseline model.

The router uses a request-value signal to group requests into segments based on predicted likelihood of user engagement with the ad. An explore-and-exploit process periodically measures the incremental outcome of using the more powerful model in each segment and updates the allocation between the two models. This is necessary because the incremental benefit of the more powerful model does not always align with the absolute value of a request. The process also preserves exploratory traffic across segments so the system continues to collect the observations needed to adapt, rather than reinforcing an outdated routing decision.

A calibration loop keeps the realized traffic share close to its target as the traffic mix changes across regions and over time. When capacity contracts, the central controller reduces the target coverage and the client routes fewer requests to the more powerful model. Requests removed from the opportunistic path continue through the baseline model.

Multi-Layer Value-Aware Load Shedding

The RMA and SBM feedback loops continuously align opportunistic work with available capacity, but their central components operate on the order of minutes. A sudden preemption can therefore remove capacity before clients receive new targets. The system adds value-aware protection for both workloads that can react immediately:

Server-side shedding: If the opportunistic pool loses capacity before the clients’ view has caught up, servers immediately remove lower-value opportunistic work. For RMA, they reduce the number of candidates processed within individual requests; SBM applies an equivalent value-aware shedding policy to requests routed to the more powerful model. This absorbs rapid changes close to the serving bottleneck.

Client-side shedding: The RMA and SBM clients use the latest controller targets as the guideline but also observe the server status directly. When it’s observed that the server is overloaded, clients shed lower-value opportunistic work directly, i.e., RMA requests fewer additional ads, while SBM routes fewer requests to the more powerful model.

Both forms of load shedding react within a few milliseconds, bridging the interval before the controller-client loops converge. Both server-side shedding and client-side shedding use value signals when selecting work to remove, which minimizes the effect during the transition.

Current Work and What Comes Next

Increasing Workload Elasticity

We aim to use more opportunistic capacity productively by extending the operating range of RMA and SBM and broadening the set of elasticity levers. For RMA, this means supporting higher candidate volumes across ranking stages; for SBM, using more powerful models that turn additional accelerator capacity into better predictions. We are also developing new levers such as precomputation elasticity, which performs work ahead of request time and is therefore less constrained by the location and timing of live traffic.

Expanding the Usable Capacity Pool

Opportunistic capacity is fragmented across regions and accelerator types, and it’s useful only when compatible models and supporting resources are available in the same place. We are expanding model portability and cross-region inference capabilities so that more of the available capacity can be used efficiently.

Automating Value-Based Capacity Allocation

The incremental impact of each lever changes with traffic, coverage, and the available resource mix. At a given moment, the next unit of opportunistic capacity may surface more relevant ads by ranking additional candidates or by routing more requests to a powerful model. We are building an optimization-based system to automatically adjust the allocation of AI inference capacity to its possible elasticity levers based on the benefits to users and advertisers. The goal is to maximize the return of the capacity subject to the constraints that each use case has in terms of regional constraints, hardware compatibility, and durability requirements for the idle capacity, among others.

Acknowledgments

This work reflects critical contributions from a cross functional v-team across Meta:

David Amsallem, Mohit Bharti, Maddie Digne, Stephen Dimmick, Maomao Ding, Amit Dutta, Sebin George, Aashik Gowda, Atul Goyal, Mohak Goyal, Nelson Guo, Tiger Hao, Yaning Huang, Dianshi Li, Yang Li, Bai Liu, Bofeng Liu, Wei Liu, Yisi Liu, Daniel Molina Hurtado, Maciej Naruszewicz, Arka Pal, Annan Pan, Brian Park, Brian Peschka, Michael Shao, Bikash Sharma, Alexander Sun, Weiman Sun, Kaiyue Tao, Patrick Taylor, Kevin Tong, Ellie Wen, Chao Xie, Lu Yang, Sihan You, Hansen Zhang, and Anthony Zhu

We also thank the following leaders for their sponsorship and support:

Neeraj Agrawal, Justin Charlap, Brian Ellis, Prabhakar Goyal, Hong Jiang, Shri Karandikar, Santanu Kolay, Uladzimir Pashkevich, Rob Schwartzberg, Eric Shan, Matt Steiner, Nathan Yan, Tak Yan, Caijie Zhang, and Alex Zhong

entries.title: NTS: Authenticated Time at Meta
entries.summary: Meta’s public time service now speaks NTS (Network Time Security, RFC 8915) at nts.meta.com. Packets are authenticated, so a device can verify the time came from us and was not modified on the way. Our NTS servers hold no per-client state. Cookie keys are derived, not stored and not replicated. We’ve open sourced everything, including [...] Read More... The post NTS: Authenticated Time at Meta app
entries.content:
• Meta’s public time service now speaks NTS (Network Time Security, RFC 8915) at nts.meta.com. Packets are authenticated, so a device can verify the time came from us and was not modified on the way.
  • Our NTS servers hold no per-client state. Cookie keys are derived, not stored and not replicated.
  • We’ve open sourced everything, including the protocol, server, client through Meta’s Time library on GitHub.
  • We’re also encouraging everyone, particularly those who maintain an NTP client on Android or iOS, to join us in enabling NTS support.

We’ve previously written about building a more accurate time service at Meta scale – migrating from ntpd to chrony, going from 10 milliseconds to 100 microseconds, and opening time.meta.com to everyone.

That work made time precise. This work makes it verifiable.

Why NTS?

NTP has been unauthenticated since 1985, like a lot of the internet’s foundational protocols. But it is also the one every certificate, token, and signature is checked against. The client sends 48 bytes, something sends 48 bytes back, and the client believes it. There is no signature and no identity.

It is not alone in that. Plenty of the internet’s foundational protocols were designed for a network where nobody was assumed to be hostile, and the industry has been retrofitting them ever since. What makes time different is that it is not just another protocol to secure. It is the input every other security decision is measured against.

For most of NTP’s life that did not matter much, because a clock being a few seconds off was an operational annoyance. Today it is load-bearing:

  • Certificate validation: notBefore and notAfter are compared against the local clock. Wrong clock, wrong answer.
  • Token and credential expiry: “Valid for 15 minutes” is a claim about a clock.
  • Replay windows: Rejecting a request older than N seconds requires knowing what time it is.
  • Log correlation and ordering: Two hosts that disagree produce a timeline that never happened.

And the check itself is circular. You can’t do X.509 notBefore/notAfter validation without knowing the current time. Effectively you’d have to disable cert time validation, or implement one of the suggested work-arounds.

There are two common workarounds. Both are bad. You can skip validation until the clock is set, which leaves a device unprotected exactly when it is most exposed. Or you can build in-slack: A certificate issued at 12:00:00 is rejected by a client whose clock reads 11:59:30, so issuers backdate notBefore by a few minutes and validators quietly widen the window at their end. Both sides are guessing at how wrong the other one is.

That was survivable when a certificate lasted 398 days. CA/Browser Forum ballot SC-081v3 changed that. The cap on newly issued publicly trusted TLS certificates dropped to 200 days in March 2026, falls to 100 days in March 2027, and reaches 47 days in March 2029 — with domain validation reuse dropping to 10 days at the same point.

At 47 days, manual certificate management stops being viable at any scale. Renewal moves to roughly monthly, and it happens unattended — usually over ACME. An automated renewal loop on a host with a skewed clock does not raise a ticket. It reissues, or it fails, on a schedule nobody is watching.

How NTS Works

NTS works in phases, and separating them is what makes it deployable.

Phase 1 – Key Establishment (NTS-KE): TLS 1.3 over TCP/4460, negotiated with ALPN ntske/1. The client and server agree on an AEAD algorithm, then derive two directional session keys (C2S and S2C) straight from the TLS session using the RFC 5705 exporter. The server issues eight cookies, tells the client which NTP server to actually use via a server negotiation record, and closes the connection. This happens once, not per packet.

We negotiate three AEADs: AES-SIV-CMAC-256 (ID 15), which RFC 8915 makes mandatory to implement and is what an unknown client is most likely to ask for; AES-SIV-CMAC-512 (17); and AES-128-GCM-SIV (30). Client preference wins.

Phase 2 – Authenticated NTP: Standard NTPv4 over UDP/123 to the advertised server, with NTS extension fields. A request carries a unique identifier, a cookie, and an authenticator; the authenticator covers everything before it, but encrypts nothing. The server opens the cookie to recover the session keys, verifies that authenticator, and replies with the unique identifier echoed back plus an authenticator of its own – and that one does carry a payload: the fresh cookies, encrypted inside it.

A forged packet fails verification and is dropped. We do not send an NTS NAK, so a failure is indistinguishable from packet loss and cannot be used to push a client into a fresh key exchange. A replayed response carries the wrong unique identifier and matches no outstanding request. Because the replacement cookies ride inside the response authenticator rather than in the clear, an observer sees a different opaque blob every exchange and cannot follow a client between networks. Spending each cookie once is the client’s side of that bargain – the server is stateless and does not track them.

Cookies Without State

A cookie is a server state handed to the client for safekeeping. It holds the session keys, sealed with AES-SIV so only the server can open it. The obvious implementation is a key ring replicated to every server, which turns time service into a distributed state problem.

We do not replicate keys. Each server derives the sealing key from a shared master secret and the current day:

key = HKDF-SHA256(master, salt = BE32(day), info = “fbnts-cookie-seal-v1”)



Since the Unix epoch, day is measured as whole 24-hour periods,  not a calendar day. So there is no timezone and no DST, and every host computes the same integer for the same instant. That integer is the cookie’s key ID and travels in the clear. A server that has been handed a cookie it has never seen or sealed by a host it has never talked to, re-derives the key and opens it. We accept two days back and one forward to cover skew around a rotation boundary.

The result is no key ring, no replication, no session table, no shared state to fall out of sync, and nothing for an attacker to exhaust. It is also what makes the split above work – the KE server and the NTP servers it hands you off to are different machines in different places, and they never exchange anything. Adding a server is adding a server.

The plain NTP path is untouched. The responder parses extension fields only when they are present, so unauthenticated clients hit the same code as before at the same cost.

Using NTS

One line of chrony config:

pool nts.meta.com nts iburst maxsources 5

nts.meta.com terminates key exchange only. During the handshake it advertises an NTP responder in a server negotiation record, so the client is steered to time.meta.com and sends its authenticated NTP there. The host you configure is not the host you end up talking to.

That indirection is why we use pool rather than server. A single server line gives you one association and one responder, which is a single point of failure – and NTP is a protocol that wants several sources so it can outvote a bad one. pool asks for maxsources independent associations. Each runs its own key exchange over its own TLS session, so each ends up with a distinct pair of session keys:

$ chronyc authdata
Name/IP address Mode KeyID Type KLen Last Atmp NAK Cook CLen
time1.meta.com NTS 5 30 128 27 0 0 8 68
time2.meta.com NTS 7 30 128 142 0 0 8 68
time3.meta.com NTS 10 30 128 548 0 0 8 68
time4.meta.com NTS 1 30 128 1177 0 0 8 68
time5.meta.com NTS 2 30 128 1177 0 0 8 68

Five rows, five independent authenticated sources, from one line of config and one KE endpoint.

Reading across: Type 30 is the negotiated AEAD, AES-128-GCM-SIV, with KLen 128 bits of session key — chrony lists it first and client preference wins. CLen 68 is the cookie: 36 bytes of envelope around the two 16-byte keys inside. Cook 8 is cookies in hand and NAK 0 means none has been rejected.

The more interesting half is not in the table. Each row’s session keys came out of its own TLS handshake and work only for that association. The key that seals them into a cookie is the shared one – the epoch day number from the derivation above, identical on every responder we run, stamped inside each cookie and never visible to the client. That split is what lets a single key exchange hand a client five different responders that have never spoken to each other.

When a pool member completes key exchange and moves to its negotiated responder, the freed KE address is handed to the next unresolved member, repeating until maxsources responders have answered. Five sources come up in about 20 minutes as each member completes its own key exchange in turn.

NTS Protects Against Attacks

Unlike NTP, NTS stops a man-in-the-middle (MITM) attack from forging the answer. A classic MITM attack doesn’t need to break any cryptography, it just has to answer a client before a real server does. If an attacker rolls the clock backward they can make expired certificates validate again or revoked tokens work again. Any control that relies on something having expired is reset. If they roll the clock forward everything expires at once. This is the more difficult direction to address because beyond a certain point the failure stops being recoverable.

Let’s look at an example of what happens to a device that gets convinced it is the year 2037. NTP counts seconds in a 32-bit field that wraps in February 2036, and a client stranded on the far side of that boundary computes its correction into the wrong era – so the mechanism that exists to fix a wrong clock now moves it further away. Meanwhile every certificate the device holds is long expired, so TLS fails, therefore it cannot reach anything that might help, including its own update service. The patch that would fix it cannot be delivered, because delivering it needs the clock that is broken.

The device is not damaged. Every component works exactly as designed. It is simply holding a number that puts it outside the reach of the network. And no amount of waiting or rebooting fixes it. Recovery means a factory reset, or a trip to a service center. Multiply that by a fleet and the cost of a wrong integer becomes a logistics problem.

Now, consider a clock forward attack on a host that issues credentials. Short-lived credentials are considered safe because they expire quickly, which means short lifetime is doing the job revocation would otherwise do. That property is entirely a function of the issuing host’s clock. An issuer convinced it is next year signs credentials that outlive the window you designed for.

What NTS Does Not Fix

Delay attacks. RFC 8915 is explicit. An attacker who holds your packets shifts your clock by up to half the delay introduced, and no cryptography in the protocol detects it, because every byte is genuine. Authentication tells you who wrote a packet, not how long it spent in flight. Mitigations are the usual ones – multiple independent sources, sanity limits, bounded steps.

So the claim is narrow: An on-path attacker can still delay your packets and can still drop them. What they can no longer do is lie about the contents.

Bootstrapping. NTS-KE runs over TLS and TLS wants a working clock, which is the same circular problem as above. A device with a dead RTC still has to get roughly correct before its first handshake.

Wrong servers. NTS authenticates the path, not the answer. A server that is correctly configured, correctly authenticated, and simply wrong will hand you the wrong time with a perfect signature on it. Quorum, sanity checks, and monitoring are still required.

Monotonicity. Authenticated time is still wall-clock time, and wall clocks move backward — at a leap second, or whenever a correction lands. Cloudflare’s authoritative DNS hit this at the end of 2016: a resolver round-trip measured across the leap second came out negative, propagated into upstream selection, and panicked Go’s rand.Int63n(). Nothing was forged and nothing was misdelivered. If your code measures elapsed time, use a monotonic clock.

Adoption

RFC 8915, Network Time Security for the Network Time Protocol, was published on the IETF Standards Track as a Proposed Standard in September 2020. Cloudflare had launched time.cloudflare.com with NTS 15 months earlier, in June 2019, against the then-current draft, and showed it works at scale.

Server-side, the public NTS list today runs to a few dozen entries, mostly national metrology institutes and internet infrastructure operators such as PTB, Netnod, and time.nl. We are adding one more.

The bigger gap is on the client. NTS support exists where you would expect it in the server world – chrony and ntpsec implement it. It is absent entirely from the stock time client on the platforms that account for most of the endpoints on the internet.

Android’s platform time sync is plain SNTP over UDP/123 – a fixed 48-byte packet with no extension-field handling, alongside NITZ and GNSS – so there is no NTS path in it. Apple devices sync through timed against time.apple.com, where we are not aware of any NTS support either.

Those two stacks set the clock on billions of phones, watches and headsets, and every one of them is trusting an unauthenticated UDP packet. A device vendor can ship a separate NTS-capable client today — chrony runs perfectly well on Android – but that is a workaround for something the platform should do itself.

The protocol is finished, the servers are appearing, the client implementations exist.

What is missing is mobile.

Join Us in Enabling NTS

nts.meta.com is live and free. The code is in github.com/facebook/time.

If you run a public time service, turn NTS on. If you maintain an NTP client, implement RFC 8915. If you own the time stack in a mobile OS, this is the gap – Android and iOS are where most of the world’s clocks get set, and both of them are still doing it over an unauthenticated packet.

We have spent years making time more precise. Precision without authenticity only gets you a very accurate number from an unknown source. Now it can be both.

Acknowledgements

We’d like to thank Sofia Scalzo, Pablo Mazzini, Vadim Fedorenko, Patrick Cullen, and Yixin Wei for their support on this project.
